content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes PPCVGAE to learn privacy-preserving graph embedding against sensitive attribute inference. Specifically, PPCVGE extends to VGAE to conditional VGAE by introducing the sensitive attributes to learn node embedding. To make sure that node embedding is privacy-preserving, PPCVGE adds a privacy penalty. It further adds differential privacy noise to the node embedding. The paper considers two scenarios: (a) the adversary only know part of sensitive attributes; and (b) the adversary know part of sensitive attributes and graph structure.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The problem of learning privacy-preserving node embedding against sensitive attribute inference attack is important
2. The paper considers two scenarios
3. In general, the paper is easy to understand

Weaknesses:
1. The novelty and contributions of the proposed method is incremental. Extending VGAE to CVGE to include sensitive attributes is straightforward. The proposed privacy penalty is interesting but not surprising.

2. Experiments are incomplete. First, some important baselines are missing such as adversarial training based [1]. Though the authors claim adversarial training is difficult to train, adversarial training based privacy preserving node representation learning is still a strong baseline that the authors should be included. Second, the authors only conduct experiments when 30% of sensitive attributes are publicly available. The authors are encouraged to vary the percentage of the public sensitive attributes to fully evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method under various conditions.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: In general, the paper is easy to follow. However, the novelty of the paper is limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper studies an important problem of learning privacy-preserving node embedding. However, the novelty and contributions of the paper are increment and experiments need to be improved.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the problem of privacy-preserving graph embedding learning. The intended application scenario is that a graph owner learns node embeddings of his/her graph, where private nodes do not share the value of their sensitive attributes with downstream users. The proposed solution is motivated by the notion of differential privacy, and solutions under different assumptions about the attacker are provided, i.e., when the attackers know the graph structure and sensitive attributes of public nodes or when the attackers only know the sensitive attributes of public nodes. Experiments on five public graph datasets were performed, where both the level of privacy preserving and utility are evaluated.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
+ Given the prevalence of application of graph neural networks and releasing of large-scale graph data, the necessity and importance of this proposed research are self-evident. This is a big plus of this work.
+ The paper is generally well-written and easy to follow about its main intuition and key methodology. 

Weakness:
- I am not fully convinced the proposed solution rigorously implemented differential privacy. And hence it might be over claiming. Although Section 5 talks a lot about differential privacy, what it actually does is to introduce a regularization term, i.e., the so-called privacy penalty, to require the variational mean vector obtained with sensitive attributes from private nodes to be closer to the variational mean vector obtained without sensitive attributes from private nodes. Hence, this regularization has nothing to do with differential privacy. 
- Even with the so-called “to achieve exact $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP”, it is never clear how the sensitivity parameter $\Delta \nu$ is calculated. Shall we exhaust all possible privacy candidates to obtain the exact variance of variational mean vector to compute $\Delta \nu$? Or there will be some clipping in the estimated variational mean vector to bound its norm, so that the sensitivity parameter $\Delta \nu$ is simply bounded by a constant? 
- In Section 4.2, the authors made a very strong assumption that $P(X,A|Z,s)= P(X|Z,s)P(A|Z,s)$. I guess this could be true only when we have ground-truth node embedding $Z$. But when we are conditioning on the learnt embeddings, this might not hold. If this does not hold, the privacy guarantee might not hold, as the sensitivity is based on the learnt embeddings. The observations in the reported experiments seem also suggest so: on graphs where node features are strongly correlated with connectivity, the proposed privacy protection mechanism does not really work. In these cases, even when direct noise is injected to the learnt embeddings, the privacy is not achieved (as $\epsilon$ was set to 0.01). This looks very suspicious. 
- In Section 6.2, it is mentioned that the privacy candidate set is built by setting $s’_i$ to the opposite of the ground-truth label for $i\in P$. But when the sensitive attribute takes multiple values, such as region, how to set $s’_i$? And for any differential privacy related work, it is very important to vary the privacy parameter, i.e., $\epsilon$ and $\delta$, to observe how the model performs accordingly. Unfortunately, only one setting of $\epsilon$ and $\delta$ are used in all the experiments. 
- Some of the experiment results are also very suspicious. For example, in Table 2, on Recidivism dataset, PPCVGAE+DP for case (b)’s F1 performance is only 0.14+/-0.20; and for the same method on Credit defaulter dataset, the variance is more than 17. And in Table 3, PPCVGAE+DP for case (a)’s performance on Credit defaulter dataset is very high, basically means the added Gaussian noise failed to protect privacy, though it worked well on other datasets.  

Question:
- Can the authors explain why cannot we simply add Gaussian or Laplacian noise to the learnt embeddings from a GNN model (e.g., GCN) to obtain desired differential privacy? Or one can simply use DP-SGD and leveraging the post-processing invariant property of DP to achieve differential privacy?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is in general clearly explained, except the privacy part, which lacks necessary rigor. Specifically, Section 5 starts with differential privacy, which leaves the audience the impression that this would be the privacy guarantee provided; but unfortunately, the main method actually introduced has nothing to do with differential privacy. This could be misleading. It is also unclear how the sensitivity parameter $\Delta \nu$ is actually calculated, which is important for the follow up research to reproduce the results in this paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper targets a very important problem in practice, i.e., privacy preserving release of learnt graph embeddings. However, the proposed solution lacks necessary rigor in the privacy to be achieved, and the reported experiment results are also suspicious and incomplete to support the arguments made in the paper.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a privacy preserving conditional variational graph autoencoder (CVGAE) that can learn / generate graph embeddings that can satisfy differential privacy. Their embeddings preserve graph structure information and non-sensitive features which can be used for downstream tasks while being insensitive to the changes of sensitive attributes. They compare against a competing method and a baseline that is a standard VGAE with non privacy preserving embeddings.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Paper is well written with solid foundations for their proposed model
- Paper considers an interesting problem and has a novel solution

Weaknesses:
- The DP-GCN by Hu et al. does not seem to be privacy preserving at all? In many datasets, it has worse privacy performance than the baseline VGAE, but isn't this method supposed to be somewhat privacy preserving? In the related works, it is mentioned that there can be privacy leakage in their method, but even a method with leakage should still be better than a baseline method that doesn't do any privacy preservation at all? This makes it a bit suspicious that the experiments aren't convoluted in a certain way to make the paper's proposed models more favorable looking. 
- Why is DP-GCN not shown for case b) which is the simpler / easier case with a weaker adversary?
- It doesn't make sense to compare case a) and case b) together and pick the best model from both cases as the cases represent different adversary scenarios
- It is not immediately clear that the bolded values represent the best trade-off between utility and privacy. It is also kind of werid to show a trade-off as two separate tables.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Clarity is good, quality and novelty seem good
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall the paper is well-presented and the technical details seem strong. The experiment results seem kind of strange (see above) and there isn't a lot of competing models to compare against, although if that is due to novelty of the problem, there isn't really anything that can be done about that.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 4: The contributions are significant, and do not exist in prior works.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
